Tennessee Eastman unit: an interactive process tour

Prototype · placeholder geometry · recorded replay

A walk through a published benchmark process for new-operator orientation. Pick a unit to see why it exists, which instruments to watch and what the recorded replay shows. The connections, tags, purpose sentences, alarm limits and every number come from this repository's data files; shapes, sizes, heights and pipe routes are placeholders.

Pulses move in the flow direction given by the model. Their speed follows the recorded flow where the stream has a flow tag (FI-101, FI-102, FI-103, FI-104, FI-106, FI-105, FI-110, FI-114, FI-117); other lines move at a constant, illustrative rate. Cooling water and steam are inferred from valve descriptions; they are not streams in the model.

  • in normal band
  • outside normal band (display aid, not a limit)
  • above a published alarm limit
  • not connected (no replay source)

Design mockup, not a procedure. Isolation points inferred from the TE seed model; not a lockout/tagout procedure (a real one comes from the site's energy-control program, OSHA 1910.147, verified P&IDs and an authorized person). Nothing here may be used as a lockout/tagout procedure.

Select inferred isolation points to see which energy sources remain and where flow stops, computed from the stream graph. The pulses here run at a constant rate; they are not the replay.

What this is and is not

Prototype. A published benchmark process, the Tennessee Eastman process, stands in for a plant. Shapes, sizes, positions and pipe routes are placeholders; the stream connections are checked against the simulator code but not reviewed by an operator; tag colours come from a recorded replay, not a live plant. The script was written by an AI assistant from the repository's data files and has not been reviewed by an operator.

The tour's text around the numbers (the short function lines, captions and this page) was written with AI assistance from the data files; each purpose sentence comes from data/te_unit_purposes.json, which cites the simulator lines it restates. Nothing here has been reviewed by an operator. Hazard citations are a prototype keyword match against public incident records: mechanism analogies, not a hazard analysis.

Data: Tennessee Eastman process after Downs and Vogel (1993); simulator code and recorded runs by the Large Scale Systems Research Laboratory (Professor Richard Braatz, Director), University of Illinois.
